summary:
For 25 years, NASA’s MODIS instruments have recorded wildfires worldwide, building the long-term record behind fire trend analysis, risk models and resource planning. MODIS ends science operations in 2027, and its successor, VIIRS, sees fire differently: its sharper resolution detects smaller fires. Switching directly from one to the other would make fire activity appear to jump when nothing has changed on the ground.

1. Risk models could flag communities as more fire-prone than they are, pushing up insurance costs. 

2. Health and emergency budgets get planned around a crisis that isn’t real. 

3.  firefighters get sent where the data looks worst, not where the fires are.

FireCal solves this through data harmonization and prediction. Using 2012–2026, when both instruments observed the same fires, we learn how their readings differ and translate new VIIRS data into MODIS-equivalent values. The result is one continuous record from 2000 onward. Our predictive model trains on this harmonized history and keeps forecasting fire activity after MODIS goes dark. 

Our prototype includes a display of past data, predictive data, and a potential for live data viewing.
details:
It shows MODIS and VIIRS data harmonized for easier view. It also makes predictions based on would-be MODIS data to show a more accurate VIIRS output. The intended impact is to ease the transition to a VIIRS-only era, so that 25 years of MODIS fire history stays usable and the trends, risk assessments and forecasts built on it remain accurate after MODIS shuts down.

The tools we used are Github and Claude code with Python, VS Code.

The creative aspect was the predictive aspect, because it goes beyond the scope of pure harmonization and goes into the actual usefulness of the system.
